title: Conditions, Part Two
subtitle: Future, general, and mixed conditions.
objectives: Form and translate future-more-vivid conditions (ἐάν + subjunctive, future).
Form and translate future-less-vivid conditions (εἰ + optative, optative + ἄν).
Form and translate present and past general conditions.
Master all six types of Greek conditional sentences.

sections.heading: The remaining four condition types
sections.body: Today we complete the system of Greek conditionals. You have learned simple particular and contrary-to-fact. Now you will learn future-more-vivid, future-less-vivid, present general, and past general. Once you have all six, you can parse and translate any conditional sentence in Greek prose.

sections.heading: Future-more-vivid
sections.body:
ἐάν + subjunctive, future indicative

ἐὰν λύῃς, ἀγαθὸς ἔσῃ.
'If you loose (and you may), you will be good.'

The future-more-vivid condition expresses a likely future condition. ἐάν (= εἰ + ἄν) is used with the subjunctive in the protasis, and the future indicative appears in the apodosis. This is the most common future condition in Greek.

sections.heading: Future-less-vivid
sections.body:
εἰ + optative, optative + ἄν

εἰ λύοις, ἀγαθὸς εἴης ἄν.
'If you should loose (but you probably won't), you would be good.'

The future-less-vivid condition expresses a remote or unlikely future condition. The optative appears in both protasis and apodosis, with ἄν in the apodosis. This condition is less common than the future-more-vivid.

sections.heading: Present general
sections.body:
ἐάν + subjunctive, present indicative

ἐὰν λύῃς, ἀγαθὸς εἶ.
'If you loose (whenever you do), you are good (always).'

The present general condition expresses a repeated or habitual action in present time. The subjunctive appears in the protasis; the present indicative appears in the apodosis. This condition states a general truth: whenever X happens, Y happens.

sections.heading: Past general
sections.body:
εἰ + optative, imperfect indicative

εἰ λύοις, ἀγαθὸς ἦσθα.
'If you loosed (whenever you did), you were good (always).'

The past general condition expresses a repeated or habitual action in past time. The optative appears in the protasis; the imperfect indicative appears in the apodosis. This condition states a general truth about the past: whenever X happened, Y happened.

sections.heading: Summary of all six types
sections.body:
1. Simple particular: εἰ + indicative, indicative
2. Contrary-to-fact: εἰ + secondary tense, ἄν + secondary tense
3. Future-more-vivid: ἐάν + subjunctive, future
4. Future-less-vivid: εἰ + optative, optative + ἄν
5. Present general: ἐάν + subjunctive, present
6. Past general: εἰ + optative, imperfect

Memoriz these six patterns. Every Greek conditional sentence falls into one of these types.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 4.7 introduces indirect statement. Greek has three ways to express indirect statement: ὅτι + indicative, accusative + infinitive, and accusative + participle. You will learn all three here.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can recognize and translate all six types of Greek conditional sentences and can produce them correctly in Greek.
